Outcome: Depression cases (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Working people with vitamin D deficiency had a higher prevalence of moderate depression than those with other vitamin D statuses.
Sentence: "The overall prevalence of moderate depression was 15%, with higher prevalence among working women compared to men [χ 2 (df) = 6.7(1), P=0.01], those practicing religions other than Hinduism [χ 2 (df) = 5.5(1), P=0.01], those educated up to primary school compared to other education criteria [χ 2 (df) = 9.4(4), P=0.03], those having vitamin D deficiency compared to others [χ 2 (df) = 8.5(3), P=0.03], and sedentary lifestyle compared to active lifestyle [χ 2 (df) = 6.7(1), P=0.009]."
Measured as: moderate depression (BDI-Ia score ≥20)
Population: Paid working population in Nepal (n=160)
Intervention: Vitamin D status (deficiency vs others), observed not given
Comparator: Participants without vitamin D deficiency
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 160
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: harm
Claim: Vitamin D level was significantly related to risk of depression (PHQ-9 above 5) six months after COVID-19 hospital admission; the direction is not stated in the abstract.
Sentence: "The variables that were significantly related to the risk of depression 6 months after admission for COVID-19 were frailty (p = 0.006 for pre-frail and p = 0.001 for frail), small-vessel vascular disease in imaging tests (p = 0.033), vitamin D level (p = 0.006), and taking antidepressants (p = 0.011)."
Measured as: risk of depression (PHQ-9 above 5)
Population: 72 patients admitted to a hospital in Spain for COVID-19, assessed at discharge and six months later
Intervention: Serum vitamin D level (measured, not administered)
Comparator: Lower versus higher vitamin D levels across participants
Design: cohort study
Sample size: 72
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"rationale":"Both are observational studies linking vitamin D status to depression in different populations with different instruments and cut-offs; the abstract does not state Study B's direction, so the conflict is real but hard to pin on one cause.","verdict":"genuine","reason":"population","also_differs":["outcome_measure","design_or_bias"],"detail":"healthy-ish working adults in Nepal (BDI-Ia >=20) vs post-COVID hospital patients in Spain (PHQ-9 >5)"}
